title: Lists, factors, display and formatting in R
breadcrumb: Module 9 · R Programming · Lists, factors and formatting
objectives: Create and index lists, including nested elements.
Understand factors, levels and ordered factors.
Interpret print, str, class, summary and formatting functions.
Recognise factor-code versus label and display-versus-data traps.

prereq.name: R objects and classes
prereq.why: Display functions reveal object structure and class.

traps: A list can contain objects of different types and lengths.
x[i] returns a sublist; x[[i]] returns the element itself.
x$name is shorthand for extracting a named list element.
A factor stores integer codes plus levels; codes are not necessarily the printed labels.
factor() levels are ordered alphabetically by default unless levels are supplied.
ordered=TRUE creates an ordered factor with level order.
as.numeric(factor) returns internal codes, not the original numeric labels.
str() displays structure; class() reports class; levels() reports factor labels.
format() returns character strings for display; it does not change the underlying numeric object.

sheet: list() creates a list that can contain heterogeneous objects.
x[i] returns a sublist; x[[i]] extracts one element.
x$name extracts a named element; names(x) returns element names.
factor(x) encodes categories as integer codes with character levels.
levels(f) gives labels; nlevels(f) counts levels.
Specify levels= to control order and include unused categories.
as.numeric(f) returns internal integer codes, not numeric labels.
str() inspects structure; class() returns class; summary() summarises object.
format() and sprintf() create character representations for display.
Display formatting does not modify the underlying numeric value.
tricks: Use [[ ]] when a single element is required.
Inspect levels before interpreting factor codes.
Specify levels for a meaningful category order.
Do not confuse formatted strings with numeric values.
shortcuts: Write down list names and element types.
Separate factor codes from displayed labels.
Check whether a factor is ordered.
Read formatting output as character text.
remember: [ ] keeps a list; [[ ]] extracts an element.
formatting changes display, not stored values.

howto: Inspect the object with str() and class(). For lists, decide whether the question wants a sublist or a single element. For factors, read levels before interpreting codes. For display functions, distinguish a character representation from the original data.

scenes.title: Lists hold heterogeneous objects
body: A list is a recursive object that can contain elements of different types and lengths.
Use list() to create a list. Elements can be accessed by position or name.
str() is useful for inspecting the structure before extracting values.

items.recall: A container that can hold objects of different types and lengths.
refresh: A list is a recursive R object whose elements may be numeric vectors, character strings, matrices, other lists or many other object types. It is therefore useful for storing mixed records.
Inspect a list with str() and names() before extracting an element. This reveals the nesting and element names, reducing mistakes when a question uses several levels of indexing.

items.recall: A categorical variable represented by integer codes and levels.
refresh: A factor stores categorical observations using integer codes associated with a levels attribute. The printed values are the labels, while the underlying codes identify positions in the level order.
The default level order is often alphabetical. If the category order has meaning, supply levels explicitly and use ordered=TRUE when the categories are ordinal.

items.ask: What does x[[1]] return for a list?
refresh: Double brackets extract the selected element from a list. If the first element is a numeric vector, x[[1]] returns that vector rather than a list wrapper containing it.
Single brackets have a different purpose: x[1] returns a one-element sublist. The distinction matters when a later function expects a vector, a scalar or another list.

scenes.title: A list is a container
body: For x=list(score=c(72,81),name='Asha'), x[1] returns a one-element list while x[[1]] returns the score vector.
x$name extracts the named character element.

scenario.title: A tutor stores mixed information
body: A tutor stores a numeric score vector and a character name in one list. The tutor needs the score vector itself rather than a one-element list wrapper.
Single-bracket extraction preserves list structure; double brackets extract the element.

The tutor should inspect the element names and factor levels before using the stored values in a calculation or report. A numeric conversion of a factor can expose its internal codes rather than the original category labels, so it must not be interpreted as the measurement values without checking how the factor was constructed.

ask.q: What is the difference between x[1] and x[[1]]?
ask.nudge: One returns a sublist; the other returns its element.

x[[i]] extracts one element from the list.

steps.why: Double brackets return the inner list itself.
The nested extraction reaches the numeric value.

blocks.body: factor(x) stores categorical values using integer codes and a levels attribute.
levels(f) returns the category labels; levels can be specified to control order and include unused categories.
factor(x,ordered=TRUE) creates an ordered factor; the order of levels determines the category order.

hints: The first observation is low, the second high, the third medium.

solution.why: The integer codes follow the explicit levels argument.

solution.why: Each label is replaced by its position in the level sequence.
This is the factor code vector, not a numeric measurement scale.

blocks.body: class(x) reports an object's class; str(x) displays its internal structure.
summary(x) gives a compact summary appropriate to the object's class.
These functions create character representations for display; they do not change the original numeric data.

scenes.title: Formatting is not numeric rounding
scenes.objective: Separate display text from stored values.
scenes.problem: x=12.3456; y=format(x,nsmall=2). Is y numeric or character?
hints: Check the type of its result.
scenes.answer: y is character; x remains numeric.
scenes.check: Formatting returns character output and does not overwrite x.

scenario.title: A statistician formats a reported estimate
body: A statistician needs to display a value with a fixed number of decimal places. The formatting function produces text for a report, while the original numeric variable remains available for calculations.
Formatting is not the same as replacing the underlying value with a rounded number.

The tutor should inspect the element names and factor levels before using the stored values in a calculation or report. A numeric conversion of a factor can expose its internal codes rather than the original category labels, so it must not be interpreted as the measurement values without checking how the factor was constructed.
scenario.q: Should the formatted string be used for further arithmetic?
scenario.answer: No; retain the numeric variable for calculations.

ask.q: Which function can create formatted output using a template?

solution.say: Apply format() with two decimal places.
solution.why: format() creates a character representation suitable for display.

solution.say: Check the type of the formatted result.
solution.why: The output of format() is character, not a numeric vector.
Assigning the formatted result to y does not modify x.

scenes.title: Lists and factors quick sheet
body: Lists can hold heterogeneous objects. x[i] returns a sublist; x[[i]] extracts one element; x$name extracts a named element.
Factors encode categories using integer codes and levels. levels(f) returns labels; specify levels to control order.
as.numeric(f) returns internal codes, not the original labels. Use as.character(f) for labels.
str() inspects structure; class() reports class; summary() provides a compact summary.
format() and sprintf() create character output for display; they do not modify the original numeric object.
